slides.title: Transaction Architecture
slides.transcript: Welcome to Falcon Transport. This course has three modules: transaction architecture, reliable delivery and loss recovery, and congestion control and multipathing. Together, they take about sixty minutes, including diagrams and knowledge checks. We begin with transaction architecture. You'll follow requests, packets, acknowledgements and completions across a connection while keeping the upper-layer protocol at its defined boundary. The course follows Falcon specification version one point two point zero.
slides.subtitle: Module 1 of 3 · Requests, packets, and completion boundaries

slides.title: Follow the work across a connection
slides.transcript:
A reliable transport is easier to understand when we separate the responsibilities it connects. Here, you'll learn to distinguish a Falcon transaction from a network packet, identify the roles at each endpoint, and explain what changes when a request pushes data or pulls data back.

We'll trace two short examples with concrete sequence numbers. Then we'll connect those examples to resource independence and compatibility between versions. The animations deliberately spread events apart so you can inspect their consequences. Their spacing is explanatory, not a measurement of network latency.

This course has three modules. Module one examines transaction architecture. Module two examines reliable delivery and loss recovery. Module three examines congestion control and multipathing. Allow about twenty minutes per module, or sixty minutes for the full course. The optional links provide further context and are outside that estimate.

Our scope is the transport protocol. Upper-layer operation mappings, application interfaces, drivers, hardware implementation, and programming details stay outside the course. You can pause narration, inspect a completed diagram, and replay a sequence whenever a distinction needs another look.
slides.subtitle: Identify roles and sequence spaces. Trace push and pull. Explain resources and compatibility.

slides.title: Two layers, four peer roles
slides.transcript:
Falcon separates transaction responsibilities from packet delivery responsibilities. That separation explains why one event can finish at one layer while work remains at another.

The transaction sublayer handles requests and responses, transaction ordering, and resource management. A transaction begins with an upper-layer protocol request and ends with a response or completion delivered back to that protocol. We'll abbreviate upper-layer protocol as U L P. Its operation semantics remain outside Falcon's transport boundary.

The packet delivery sublayer handles reliable packet delivery, congestion control, and multipath load balancing. It sends packets, tracks feedback, and repairs losses. These responsibilities support transactions, but a packet arrival is not automatically a completed transaction.

Four role names keep the two views clear. Initiator and target name the transaction peers. Transmitter and receiver name the packet-delivery peers for a particular direction. These are roles, not four separate devices. An initiator can transmit one packet and receive another within the same transaction.

A pull makes that change easy to see. The initiator sends a request toward the target. Later, the target transmits response data back to the initiator. The transaction roles stay fixed while the packet roles reverse.

Keep that distinction whenever you read a trace. First ask which transaction is being served. Then ask which side is transmitting this particular packet. We won't derive an application interface, a driver architecture, or an upper-layer operation mapping from the diagram. Those would require contracts beyond the transport model taught here.

figure.alt: Transaction and packet delivery sublayers between opaque upper-layer boundaries.
figure.caption: Transaction roles stay fixed; packet roles depend on direction.

entries.text: Packet roles reverse when Pull Data returns.

slides.title: Connection, transaction, packet
slides.transcript:
Three different identities answer three different questions: which connection, which transaction, and which packet?

A Falcon connection is bidirectional. Each receiver allocates a destination connection identifier, or C I D, for traffic coming toward it. That destination identifier travels in the Falcon header. A source C I D is the transmitter's locally unique connection identifier and is not carried in that header. Destination identifiers don't have global meaning; the same numeric value can be allocated independently at different receivers.

Within a connection, a request sequence number, or R S N, tracks a transaction and its ordering. A packet sequence number, or P S N, tracks packet delivery. Falcon separates packet numbering into a request window for Pull Requests and a data window for Push Data and Pull Data. Don't compare a request P S N with a data P S N as though both belonged to one counter.

An ordered connection preserves the specified transaction order when delivering requests, responses, and completions. An unordered connection permits the corresponding out-of-order processing. Network arrival order and transaction delivery order are therefore different observations. We'll use ordered connections in both worked examples.

Finally, security belongs to the connection's envelope. Falcon uses P S P or I P sec E S P authentication and encryption, with a security association in each direction. That protects transferred data; it doesn't erase the distinctions among connection identity, transaction identity, and packet identity. Detailed security setup and upper-layer mappings remain outside this course.

figure.alt: Destination CID travels on the wire; RSN orders transactions; independent request and data windows assign PSNs.
figure.caption: Ordered delivery is a transaction property, not a promise of network arrival order.

slides.title: A push: receipt before acknowledgement
slides.transcript:
A push shows why received and acknowledged must remain separate states. Follow two transactions on an ordered connection. Their request sequence numbers are one and two. Packet delivery assigns data packet sequence numbers three hundred and three hundred one. The starting data base is three hundred.

Now let the network deliver packet three hundred one first. Falcon retains that later packet while the earlier transaction is missing. The two-position received bitmap becomes one zero in binary. The rightmost bit, bit zero, represents packet three hundred. The acknowledged bitmap is still zero zero. One packet has arrived, but neither push has yet earned its acknowledgement.

When packet three hundred arrives, the received bitmap becomes one one. Falcon can now deliver the two requests to the target upper-layer protocol in request-sequence order: one, then two. Even at this point, receipt alone has not changed the acknowledged bitmap.

The target upper-layer protocol now acknowledges both push requests. This boundary event allows Falcon to acknowledge their Push Data packets. Once both are acknowledged, the cumulative data base advances to three hundred two.

The acknowledgement returns to the initiator. Falcon delivers the two push completions in request-sequence order. The upper-layer protocol still owns operation-level completion semantics.

Pause on the finished sequence and trace the dependency backward. Initiator completion follows the returning acknowledgement. That acknowledgement follows target upper-layer acknowledgement. Network receipt is necessary, but is an earlier event. The same identifiers stay attached to the work throughout, even though packets arrived in the opposite order.

figure.alt: Two push packets arrive in reverse order; receive bits change before acknowledgement and ordered completion.
figure.caption: Source identifiers; event spacing is illustrative. Bit 0 corresponds to PSN 300.

Both Push Data packets can be acknowledged

slides.title: A pull: an ACK is not the response
slides.transcript:
A pull changes the direction of data, but keeps transaction identity stable. Begin with two Pull Requests, using request sequence numbers one and two. Their request-window packet numbers are one hundred and one hundred one.

Suppose request one hundred one reaches the target first. The ordered connection retains it until request one hundred arrives, then presents the requests to the target upper-layer protocol in request-sequence order. Packet delivery can acknowledge receipt of these request packets. In this example, one coalesced request acknowledgement advances the request base to one hundred two.

That acknowledgement is not the pull response. It reports request-packet delivery. The requested data still has to be produced and returned. Treating the request acknowledgement as returned data would collapse two different stages of the transaction.

Next, the target upper-layer protocol supplies the responses. Falcon sends Pull Data using the original request sequence numbers, one and two. The target's data-window packet numbers are two hundred and two hundred one. These numbers belong to a separate packet sequence space from the request numbers.

The transaction initiator is now the packet receiver. The transaction target is now the packet transmitter. At the initiator, Falcon delivers the responses in request-sequence order and acknowledges the returned data packets. This closes the transport exchange while leaving operation-level semantics with the upper-layer protocol.

Compare the two returning paths in the finished diagram. The request acknowledgement confirms that requests arrived. Pull Data carries the response and preserves the transaction's request sequence number. The two arrows have different jobs, even though both travel toward the initiator.

figure.alt: Two Pull Requests use request PSNs 100 and 101; their responses use data PSNs 200 and 201.
figure.caption: RSNs 1 and 2 persist across the change in packet direction.

slides.title: Reserve metadata. Allocate buffers on arrival.
slides.transcript:
Forward progress depends on keeping resources independent where the protocol needs them. Transmit and receive resources serve different directions. Packet metadata and payload buffers serve different purposes. Requests and responses also need protected capacity so one class of work cannot consume everything required to finish another.

Head of line, or H o L, means the next transaction whose progress unblocks an ordered stream. Resource protections preserve progress for that work even under pressure. The specification describes separate resource regions and head-of-line provisions; our diagram shows their protocol purpose, not a particular allocator or hardware design.

Now follow a version one point two pull with request sequence number seven. When initiating the request, Falcon proactively reserves the required receive packet metadata in the upper-layer requests region. That metadata lets the later response be matched with its outstanding request. It has not been removed by on-demand buffering.

While the response is pending, don't picture the full response payload buffer as already reserved. When Pull Data arrives, Falcon validates its outstanding request and allocates receive buffer resources from the network region, using the receive packet metadata reserved earlier.

Consider a separate admission-failure case. If receive buffers are unavailable, Falcon discards that data packet and generates a resource negative-acknowledgement event. No delivery or completion occurs from that rejected arrival.

Compatibility preserves another distinction. When interoperating with a version one point zero or one point one peer, the target must gate Pull Responses on the Nick congestion window, called n c window, for performance. Negotiation doesn't give an older receiver the newer resource behavior. Reservation, arrival-time allocation, and successful admission remain three different facts.

figure.alt: Pull-response metadata is reserved at initiation and network receive buffers are allocated on arrival, with a separate failed-admission case.
figure.caption: Independent resources protect head-of-line progress. Buffer admission remains necessary.

Independent Tx / Rx and request / response resources protect HoL progress.

slides.title: Negotiate behavior, not a revision number
slides.transcript:
A specification revision and a packet's Version field answer different questions. This course uses Falcon specification version one point two point zero. The base-header Version field remains one. Reading that field alone doesn't tell you which later capabilities both endpoints can use.

The control plane negotiates endpoint capabilities during connection establishment. Version one point two endpoints must interoperate with peers using version one point zero or one point one features. Compatibility means selecting supported behavior and respecting older-peer limits, not treating every feature as universally available.

Keep the chronology straight. Multipathing with up to four paths and compact congestion signaling arrived in version one point one. Congestion signaling is commonly abbreviated C S I G. Both capabilities are incompatible with a version one point zero peer, so multipathing must be disabled for that peer and C S I G cannot be assumed.

Version one point two adds the time-based recovery mechanisms, the explicit extended-acknowledgement request bit, expanded receive state, a new multipath scheduler, and on-demand pull-response resources. Older receivers ignore the new extended-acknowledgement request bit. For a version one point one receiver, the interoperability table specifies a transmit-window cap of two hundred fifty-six for performance. Don't generalize that numeric row into an unstated rule for every older peer.

The related M R C and S U E T courses explore neighboring transport ideas. They are optional context, not Falcon prerequisites or alternate names for its mechanisms. Use Falcon's own transaction, acknowledgement, resource, and compatibility rules when reasoning about Falcon. Modules two and three develop the recovery and congestion-control details from that foundation.

slides.title: Keep the evidence separate
slides.transcript:
The central skill is to keep layers and evidence separate. Initiator and target describe a transaction. Transmitter and receiver describe one packet direction. A connection identifier selects connection context, a request sequence number identifies transaction order, and packet sequence numbers belong to separate request and data windows.

For a push, packet receipt precedes target upper-layer acknowledgement, which permits the returning acknowledgement and initiator completion. For a pull, the request acknowledgement is distinct from the response data coming back.

Resource independence protects forward progress. Version one point two still reserves the receive metadata needed to match a pull response, while allocating its network receive buffer on arrival. Failed admission doesn't become successful delivery.

Finally, negotiated capabilities and interoperability limits determine what a connection can use. Keep the specification revision separate from the base-header Version field. These distinctions give you a reliable starting point for the loss-recovery and multipathing modules.
items: Transaction roles and packet-direction roles answer different questions.
RSNs track transactions; request and data windows have independent PSNs.
Push acknowledgement depends on target ULP acknowledgement.
A pull-request ACK is distinct from returned Pull Data.
Metadata reservation, buffer allocation, and admission are separate events.

slides.title: Test the transaction model
slides.transcript:
Check the transaction model before finishing. The first question asks what allows Falcon to acknowledge Push Data. The second asks you to separate the resource events in a version one point two pull and recognize the older-peer condition.

Choose one answer for the first question and every applicable answer for the second. Submit each question once to continue. Correct answers are not required, and you can retry after reading the feedback. Each explanation points to the supporting specification pages. Use those explanations to reconnect the answer to the sequence you just traced.
slides.subtitle: Submit both questions once to continue. Retry after feedback.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly describe v1.2 pull-response resources and compatibility? Select all that apply.

Network receive buffers are allocated when Pull Data arrives.

slides.title: Up next
slides.transcript: Thank you for completing module one, Transaction Architecture. You can now follow push and pull exchanges without confusing packet arrival, acknowledgement and transaction completion. Next, module two examines Reliable Delivery and Loss Recovery. It builds on the separate packet windows and received-versus-acknowledged distinction. Keep those boundaries in mind as you trace selective repair, time-based recovery and error outcomes. Continue to the next module when you're ready.

slides.title: Reliable Delivery and Loss Recovery
slides.transcript: Welcome to module two, Reliable Delivery and Loss Recovery. A packet can arrive, wait for acknowledgement, be retransmitted, or complete with an error. Those events mean different things. This module follows the evidence that lets Falcon choose the next recovery action. We will separate the two packet windows, repair one missing packet, compare time-based recovery with quiet-tail probing, and trace retry ownership and error recovery. The examples use Falcon version one point two point zero.
slides.subtitle: Module 2 of 3 · Evidence, selective repair, and forward progress

slides.title: Follow the recovery evidence
slides.transcript:
By the end of this module, you will be able to read a receiver bitmap without confusing receipt with acknowledgement. You will explain why an internal receive window and a wire bitmap have different widths. You will follow selective repair, distinguish Rack's time-based inference from a tail loss probe, and identify which endpoint owns a receiver-not-ready retry.

Finally, you will explain how Resync restores sequence progress while preserving an error completion. This is the second module in Falcon Transport. Module one established the connection and transaction model. Module three follows the measurement and path-selection loops.

The estimated twenty minutes includes narration, time to inspect the diagrams, and two questions. Numerical timing examples are illustrative, not tuning recommendations. Upper Layer Protocol actions remain boundary events. We do not examine application interfaces, mappings, drivers, or hardware implementation.
slides.subtitle: About 20 minutes · Includes inspection and knowledge checks
objectives: Read receiver state and wire feedback
Compare selective repair, RACK, and tail probes
Trace retry ownership and error recovery

slides.title: Capacity, receipt, and acknowledgement
slides.transcript:
Reliable delivery needs a precise answer to two questions: which packet arrived, and which packet may be acknowledged? Falcon separates Pull Requests into the request window and Push Data and Pull Data into the data window. Their packet sequence numbers, or P S Ns, belong to independent sequence spaces.

In version one point two, each receiver window holds five hundred twelve positions. That internal capacity does not enlarge the fields carried in an extended acknowledgement, or E ack. The wire format still provides one hundred twenty-eight data acknowledgement bits, one hundred twenty-eight data received bits, and sixty-four request bits. A feedback snapshot therefore does not describe every possible internal position at once.

For Push Data, arrival sets received state, while acknowledgement waits for the target Upper Layer Protocol, or U L P, to acknowledge the transaction. The request bitmap can serve both purposes because request receipt and acknowledgement coincide. This distinction prevents a packet waiting at the target from being mistaken for a network loss.

Two header controls also have different jobs. A R, the acknowledgement request bit, requests an acknowledgement when the packet is acknowledged. For Push Data, it does not bypass the U L P. E R, the extended acknowledgement request bit, selects E ack feedback on a supporting receiver. It does not turn receipt into transaction success.

Keep the window, state, and feedback format separate. Those three boundaries explain both selective recovery and mixed-version behavior.

cards.title: Two independent windows
cards.body: Request: Pull Request. Data: Push Data and Pull Data. Each v1.2 receive window tracks 512 positions.

cards.title: Unchanged EACK wire widths
cards.body: Data-ACK: 128 bits. Data-Rx: 128 bits. Request: 64 bits. Internal capacity is not wire width.

cards.title: Received ≠ acknowledged
cards.body: Push Data acknowledgement waits for the target ULP. Request receipt and acknowledgement coincide.

cards.title: AR and ER have separate jobs
cards.body: AR requests ACK when the packet is acknowledged. ER requests EACK on a supporting peer; it does not imply transaction success.

slides.title: Repair the hole; preserve received packets
slides.transcript:
Consider four Push Data packets on one path, with P S Ns three hundred through three hundred three and transaction sequence numbers one through four. The first packet is lost. The other three reach the receiver and remain available there while the ordered connection waits for the missing first transaction.

Read the displayed bits from right to left: bit zero, the rightmost bit, represents P S N three hundred. The data received bitmap is one one one zero in binary. The data acknowledgement bitmap is still zero zero zero zero because the target U L P has not acknowledged the ordered requests. The zero received bit identifies the network hole; the zero acknowledgement bits alone would not.

Now apply the out-of-order distance method. For this example only, assume a threshold of two and that the recency check has passed. Three hundred is less than three hundred three minus two, and the last transmission plus one round-trip time is earlier than now. The sender can select P S N three hundred for early retransmission, subject to the transmission gates.

When it arrives, received state becomes one one one one. The receiver can deliver transactions one through four in order. After U L P acknowledgement, the cumulative data base advances to three hundred four. Packets three hundred one through three hundred three are preserved, not replayed.

A small gap or a recently sent packet would not supply the same evidence. With multipathing, the distance calculation uses each packet's saved path identity. A faster different path is not sufficient evidence by itself.

figure.caption: At base 300, 1110b reports 301–303 received; bit 0 at the right represents missing PSN 300. Threshold 2 is illustrative.

slides.title: RACK tests time within known feedback
slides.transcript:
Recent Acknowledgement, or Rack, asks whether an unreceived packet has waited long enough, using time rather than sequence distance. This is a separate example of the alternative early-retransmission method. Falcon supports both method families, but selects one at system initialization. Do not combine their thresholds into a new algorithm.

Our illustrative timeline sends P S N three hundred at time zero, three hundred one at time one, and three hundred two at time two, in microseconds. At time seven, an E ack reports that the latter two packets were received. Three hundred is missing, and it lies within the reported bitmap horizon.

The latest acknowledged transmission time is two. Assume a measured round trip of four microseconds, a smoothed round trip of four, and a reordering factor of one quarter. The Rack timeout is four plus four times one quarter, or five microseconds. The missing packet was sent no later than time two, and its elapsed time is seven, which is at least five. It is eligible for the Rack loss decision, subject to transmission gating.

Three exclusions matter. A packet already reported received is excluded even if its transaction is not yet acknowledged. A packet beyond the known bitmap horizon is excluded because its received state is unknown. A packet sent after the latest acknowledged transmission time is too fresh for this inference.

For an otherwise eligible packet whose elapsed time is still below the timeout, the remaining cushion allows reordering before loss is declared. Rack is a disciplined inference from feedback and timing, not proof that every outstanding packet was dropped.

slides.title: A quiet-tail probe restarts feedback
slides.transcript:
A quiet tail creates a different problem: the sender may have too little feedback to make a useful loss decision. Tail Loss Probe, or T L P, sends a probe after a period with no transmitted or received packets. It tries to restart feedback, rather than declaring every quiet packet lost.

Reset to a new illustrative case. P S N four hundred is acknowledged, and four hundred one remains unacknowledged. Last activity occurred at time four microseconds. Assume a smoothed round trip of four, a probe factor of two, and a minimum probe timeout of six. The timeout is the maximum of eight and six, so eight microseconds.

At time twelve point one, inactivity exceeds eight. The sender retransmits the lowest unacknowledged packet in that window, four hundred one, as the probe. It sets both A R and E R. If both request and data windows have outstanding work, probing is considered per window. The returned feedback can then support Rack recovery when its conditions hold.

Compatibility changes the feedback expectation. A version one point zero or one point one receiver ignores E R. T L P falls back to A R-triggered acknowledgement behavior; an immediate E ack is not guaranteed. A R still respects packet acknowledgement semantics, including U L P acknowledgement for Push Data.

The larger receive window is a separate compatibility issue. With a version one point one receiver, cap the transmit window at its two hundred fifty-six positions for performance. Do not infer five hundred twelve-position peer capacity from a version one point two sender. The backup retransmission timeout remains available.

slides.title: Retry ownership follows acknowledgement
slides.transcript:
Receiver Not Ready, or R N R, means that the target U L P cannot accept a transaction yet. The retry owner depends on whether the transaction is a push or a pull. Follow the two numbered flows separately.

For a push, the initiator sends Push Data with P S N three hundred one and transaction sequence number one. The target U L P returns R N R. Suppose the first network negative acknowledgement, or NACK, is lost. The original data packet remains unacknowledged at the initiator, so its retransmission timeout still protects progress. The initiator sends the packet again.

A later R N R NACK reaches the initiator. Retry timing now respects the indicated delay. The error-handling table specifies the maximum of the retransmission timeout and the R N R NACK timeout, rather than a shorter invented deadline. When retry becomes eligible, the initiator sends again. Once the target U L P accepts and acknowledges the push, Falcon can return the final acknowledgement and the initiator can complete it.

For a pull, the request packet can already be acknowledged before the target U L P reports R N R. The target retains the transaction, waits for the indicated delay, and redelivers the request to its own U L P. When accepted, the target sends the returned Pull Data.

This is why the pull diagram has a local retry at the target. A remote push-style retransmission loop would assign responsibility to the wrong endpoint. Packet acknowledgement has already changed what remains to be recovered.

figure.alt: Push RNR: the initiator retransmits unacknowledged data. Pull RNR: the target waits and redelivers its acknowledged request locally.
figure.caption: Push RNR: the initiator retransmits unacknowledged data. Pull RNR: the target waits and redelivers its acknowledged request locally.

entries.text: Pull Request can already be acknowledged.
Lost push NACK: original packet timeout still protects progress. Retry delay = max(RTO, RNR-NACK-timeout).

slides.title: Restore sequence progress; preserve the error
slides.transcript:
Complete In Error, or C I E, is a terminal transaction result that still needs reliable sequence progress. In the worked push flow, P S N three hundred one carries transaction sequence number one. The target U L P rejects it with C I E, and the first error NACK is lost.

The initiator eventually retransmits the unacknowledged data packet. The target recognizes its saved C I E state and returns the same error indication. It does not repeat the failed U L P operation. Once that NACK reaches the initiator, the initiator sends Resync using the original packet's P S N, transaction sequence number, and path identity.

Resync closes the sequence hole at the receiver and receives its own acknowledgement. In this worked sequence, the initiator then returns an error completion to its U L P. Sequence progress is restored, but the transaction remains failed. Pull error completion uses separate zero-length response semantics; it is not this push Resync flow.

Early recovery also has a backup. Retransmission timeouts protect packets when feedback is absent, while retry limits and error handling bound recovery. Physical packet and buffer resources are ultimately guarded and reclaimed by timeout. The specification recommends a significantly longer transaction-resource reclaim timeout than the packet-delivery timeout to prevent races. These are protocol responsibilities, not a hardware allocation recipe.

Related M R C and S U E T courses provide useful comparison. Keep their mechanisms distinct: Falcon retains out-of-order packets and selectively repairs holes, and its acknowledgement boundaries follow Falcon's rules. Do not import another transport's failure-bypass timing or gap-recovery algorithm into this sequence.

figure.alt: The repeated CIE NACK leads to Resync with the original PSN, RSN, and path-id. Its ACK closes the sequence hole; the completion remains an error.
figure.caption: The repeated CIE NACK leads to Resync with the original PSN, RSN, and path-id. Its ACK closes the sequence hole; the completion remains an error.

slides.title: Name the evidence before choosing recovery
slides.transcript:
Recovery becomes easier to reason about when every decision names its evidence. Internal window capacity tells you what the receiver can track. E ack widths tell you what one wire snapshot reports. Received state tells you whether network repair is needed; acknowledged state governs completion of packet-delivery work.

The distance method protects against ordinary reordering with both distance and recency checks. Rack instead uses reported received state, a known bitmap horizon, and transmission timing. One early method is selected at initialization. A tail loss probe supplies feedback after inactivity, with older peers using the acknowledgement-request fallback.

Finally, identify the retry owner before drawing a recovery loop. Push R N R uses initiator retransmission, while pull R N R is redelivered locally at the target. Resync repairs a sequence hole without erasing a transaction error. These distinctions let you read a trace without calling every outstanding packet lost or every acknowledgement a successful operation.

slides.title: Congestion Control and Multipathing
slides.transcript: Welcome to Falcon congestion control and multipathing, the third and final module of Falcon Transport. We will follow the feedback loop from measured packet delay to congestion windows, path selection, and protective route changes. The examples use the Falcon version one point two specification. You will see how an acknowledgment can carry both delivery information and congestion evidence, while those two jobs remain distinct. This module takes about twenty minutes including time to inspect the animations and answer two questions.
slides.subtitle: Module 3 of 3 · Measurement, control and path choice

slides.title: Follow the feedback loop
slides.transcript:
By the end of this module, you will be able to separate a packet's round trip from time spent at the receiver, explain the different jobs of the fabric and NIC congestion windows, and follow how an acknowledgment reopens capacity on a particular path.

We begin with the measurement contract between Falcon's datapath and its Rate Update Engine. We then connect Swift's control decisions and congestion signaling to the information actually returned by the network. Finally, we follow a four-path scheduling example and distinguish concurrent multipathing from a protective change of route.

Module one established Falcon's transactions and packet delivery. Module two explained selective repair and loss recovery. Here we use that context without repeating every packet format. This is a protocol course, not a tuning exercise or an implementation lab. The numerical examples help you reason about behavior; they are not recommended deployment settings. Allow time to pause at the resulting diagrams and check the arithmetic yourself.
slides.subtitle: About 20 minutes · Includes inspection and knowledge checks
objectives: Measure fabric delay and distinguish Swift control roles
Interpret compact CSIG and endpoint/fabric support
Follow per-path credit, near ties and PLB route changes

slides.title: Measure fabric delay across two clocks
slides.transcript:
A congestion controller needs a measurement that separates time in the fabric from time waiting at the receiver. Falcon's datapath collects measurements and sends events to the Rate Update Engine, or RUE. The engine returns control parameters. That contract separates observing a packet from choosing the response to its congestion evidence.

Follow the four timestamps in this example. The sender transmits at T one, with its local clock reading one hundred. The receiver records T two at five hundred ten, then transmits the acknowledgment at T three, five hundred sixteen. The sender receives that acknowledgment at T four, one hundred thirty. These are two independent clocks, with an arbitrary offset.

Subtract readings within each clock domain first. T four minus T one is thirty ticks of round-trip time. T three minus T two is six ticks of receiver residence. Subtract that residence from the round trip: thirty minus six gives twenty-four ticks of fabric delay. Each wire timestamp tick represents one hundred thirty-one point zero seven two nanoseconds, so the fabric result is three point one four five seven two eight microseconds.

The large offset between the clocks does not enter either local difference. A direct one-way subtraction, such as T two minus T one, needs synchronized clocks. With acknowledgment coalescing, Falcon uses T one and T two from the most recently received packet. Under the specified measurement assumptions, subtracting receiver residence prevents that coalescing delay from being mistaken for extra fabric delay. Keep the local differences and the cross-clock condition separate.

figure.alt: Two independent clock lanes, receiver residence and fabric-delay subtraction.
figure.caption: Subtract receiver residence: 30 − 6 = 24 ticks = 3.145728 μs.

entries.text: Datapath measurements  →  RUE events  →  control parameters
Illustrative timestamps · two independent clocks · one wire tick = 131.072 ns

slides.title: Swift separates fabric and receiver pressure
slides.transcript:
Swift uses two congestion windows because network queuing and receiver pressure are different problems. The fabric window, fcwnd, responds to measured fabric delay. The NIC window, ncwnd, responds to remote receive-resource occupancy. Falcon reports a quantized level derived from its network receive packet and buffer pools. This is protocol feedback, not a description of how to build a buffer allocator.

For ordinary acknowledgments and applicable negative acknowledgments, Swift smooths its measurements and compares them with its targets. The fabric control can increase available work when delay permits, or reduce it when delay is too high. The NIC control responds to receive pressure. A resource-exhaustion negative acknowledgment has a specific NIC-window reduction rule. Retransmission events also have a defined fabric response. A controller therefore needs the event type as well as a delay number.

Window guarding prevents repeated reactions to closely related feedback. Swift avoids reducing the fabric window repeatedly within one round trip, and avoids repeatedly changing the NIC window in the same direction within one round trip. The specification maintains time markers for those guards, including timestamp wraparound handling.

With multipathing, fabric windows are per flow, while the NIC window remains per connection. Aggregate transmission gates still apply before a path is selected. A flow with a fabric window below one uses pacing based on its round-trip time and fractional window. Only packets assigned to that sub-unity flow receive that per-flow pacing. These controls are complementary: window accounting bounds outstanding work, while pacing spaces eligible packets in time. No single feedback sample promises a fixed latency or throughput result.

figure.alt: Separate fabric and NIC control loops, with pacing and window guards.
figure.caption: Per-flow fabric control and per-connection receiver control remain distinct.

entries.text: Reduce at most once within an RTT
Only assigned packets use that pacing

slides.title: CSIG reflects a signal, not an algorithm
slides.transcript:
Congestion Signaling, or CSIG, supplies information to a transport; it does not prescribe the transport's entire congestion-control algorithm. Falcon supports the compact four-byte tag. It sits in the layer-two header, where supporting switches can record bottleneck information using compare-and-replace operations.

Trace the signal path. The sender constructs a compact tag. Switches along the packet path can update its congestion information. The receiving Falcon keeps the latest received tag state, separately for each flow when multipathing is enabled. A later acknowledgment or negative acknowledgment reflects the information back to the sender. The Rate Update Engine selects signals and processes the reflection through the congestion-event interface.

The two support conditions matter. Endpoints negotiate Falcon's CSIG capability with each other. That exchange does not negotiate switch support. The fabric must support compact CSIG end to end along the packet paths, and it should only be configured and used under that condition. An endpoint capability alone cannot establish that the network will populate the signal correctly.

CSIG and multipathing were introduced in Falcon version one point one. They are retained in version one point two; the new path scheduler does not make them new features of that revision. With a version one point zero peer, they must be disabled. Think of this reflection as a measurement channel. Swift and other supported control choices determine how measurements affect rate; the existence of a four-byte tag is not itself a rate-control policy or a guarantee of better performance.

figure.alt: Compact CSIG travels through supporting switches and is reflected to the sender.
figure.caption: Endpoint negotiation does not establish end-to-end switch support.

entries.text: Two conditions: negotiated endpoint capability + end-to-end fabric support
Endpoint negotiation does not negotiate switch support. Introduced in v1.1.

slides.title: One connection, up to four flows
slides.transcript:
Falcon can distribute a single connection across up to four flows. Each flow has a twenty-bit flow label that participates in equal-cost multipath hashing, commonly called ECMP. The lower two bits identify Falcon's path: zero zero, zero one, one zero, and one one. The flow labels must give the active paths distinct path identifiers.

Those paths do not create four independent reliable connections. Request and data delivery state remains shared at the connection level. A global delivery bitmap can describe packets that used different paths. Meanwhile, the transmitter saves the path identifier associated with each packet, and congestion measurements and fabric windows are maintained per path. This is why one acknowledgment can advance shared delivery state while generating several path-specific accounting updates.

Keep two scheduling questions separate. Connection scheduling chooses which eligible connection gets service. The path scheduler chooses a flow label for a packet of that connection after the applicable aggregate transmit gates have passed. Path selection does not override those gates, erase the two sequence windows, or change the connection's ordered-delivery contract.

The low two bits provide stable association, not a physical route certificate. A flow label influences ECMP hashing; different labels do not prove that packets traverse disjoint physical links. Later, Protective Load Balancing may change the route-selection portion of a label while preserving those path-identifier bits. The saved packet-to-path association is essential: when delivery feedback arrives, Falcon credits the path used by that packet, rather than assuming all reported packets used the path represented by the acknowledgment's congestion metadata.

figure.alt: Four low-bit path identifiers share connection delivery state.
figure.caption: Shared delivery bitmaps coexist with saved per-packet path IDs and per-path congestion metadata.

entries.text: Shared request/data delivery state and global delivery bitmaps
ACK credit returns to that path
Path: which flow carries this packet?

slides.title: An ACK reopens the original path
slides.transcript:
The version one point two Max-Open-Window scheduler selects paths using current available capacity. Assume the connection's aggregate transmit gates have passed and all four shown paths are valid. These integer windows and the ten-percent tie tolerance are illustrative.

For each path, subtract outstanding packets from its fabric window. Path zero zero has eight minus seven, leaving one. Path zero one has six minus two, leaving four. Paths one zero and one one have no open capacity. They are ineligible. The current maximum is four; with our illustrative ten-percent tolerance, the candidate threshold is three point six. Only path zero one qualifies.

Send the next packet on path zero one. Its outstanding count rises to three, so its open window falls from four to three. That is immediate path credit consumption, without waiting for a new set of software-computed weights.

Next, feedback acknowledges two previously unacknowledged packets that were originally sent on path zero zero. Their saved path identifiers direct the accounting. Its outstanding count falls from seven to five, reopening the window from one to three. Paths zero zero and zero one now tie, so round-robin tie handling selects between them. The configurable tolerance also admits sufficiently close positive windows, preventing strict maximum selection from continually favoring a slightly larger path.

A shared bitmap may acknowledge packets from several paths. Do not credit every packet to the path of the returning acknowledgment's congestion metadata. In the separate blocked case, every valid path has a nonpositive open window, so transmission waits for feedback or a window expansion. This acknowledgment-clocked scheduler replaces the earlier static weighted round-robin plan. The older scheme may be retained as an optional configuration, but it is not the normative version one point two behavior.

figure.alt: Four path cards calculate available capacity, consume credit and credit the original path.
figure.caption: Illustrative windows and 10% tie tolerance; aggregate transmit gates are assumed to pass.

slides.title: PLB changes routes after sustained congestion
slides.transcript:
Multipathing and Protective Load Balancing answer different questions. The path scheduler distributes packets among current flows. Protective Load Balancing, or PLB, decides when sustained congestion warrants changing a flow label to seek another route.

The decision has three stages. At an acknowledgment event, compare smoothed delay with the configured delay target multiplied by the configured PLB multiplier. Count how many acknowledged packets reflect congestion within the measurement round trip. If their fraction meets the configured congestion threshold, that round trip counts as congested. Count consecutive congested round trips; reaching the configured persistence threshold triggers a reroute attempt. A round trip below the congestion threshold resets the consecutive count. The animation names these thresholds rather than inventing deployment defaults.

A reroute changes the flow label's route-selection bits while preserving its low two path-identifier bits. The connection continues with the same path identity for accounting. A new label asks ECMP for a potentially different route; it does not guarantee physical diversity, a recovery time, or a throughput gain. This sustained-congestion mechanism is distinct from the failure-exclusion behavior described in the related MRC course.

Compatibility also shapes the operating mode. The version one point two sender-side scheduler is compatible with a version one point one receiver because the receiver behavior is unchanged. With a version one point zero peer, multipathing must be disabled, and compact congestion signaling is incompatible. These limits remain even when the local endpoint implements the newer scheduler. Evaluate the peer and the fabric together: a local feature does not establish an end-to-end capability.

figure.alt: Congestion fractions and consecutive congested RTTs trigger a flow-label change.
figure.caption: PLB preserves the low two path-ID bits; a new label does not guarantee a distinct physical route.

entries.text: PLB observes persistence before requesting a new route
Configured thresholds are symbolic here; these are not tuning defaults.
Below-threshold RTT resets the consecutive count.
A new ECMP label does not guarantee physical path diversity or failure recovery.
Changed route selection; same path ID
Mixed peers: v1.1 supports the v1.2 sender scheduler.
With a v1.0 peer: multipathing and CSIG must be disabled.

slides.title: Four distinctions to keep
slides.transcript:
Keep four distinctions from this module. First, a round-trip measurement includes receiver residence, so fabric-delay estimation subtracts that residence using differences within each clock. One-way delay is a separate measurement that requires synchronized clocks.

Second, fabric congestion and remote receive pressure have different controls. Swift's fabric windows are per flow under multipathing; the NIC window remains per connection. Signals, control responses, aggregate gates, path arbitration, and pacing each have a specific role.

Third, delivery state is shared but path credit is precise. An acknowledged packet reopens the path saved with that packet. The Max-Open-Window scheduler uses current capacity and round-robin handling of near ties, rather than relying on the older static weights.

Finally, Protective Load Balancing responds to persistent congestion by changing a flow label. It preserves path identity and seeks another route without promising physical diversity. When reading a design, ask what was measured, which state changed, and which endpoint and fabric capabilities support that behavior.
items: Fabric delay = sender round trip − receiver residence.
Shared delivery state; per-packet original-path credit.
Max-Open-Window schedules; PLB seeks a new route.

slides.title: Check the feedback loop
slides.transcript:
Use these two questions to check the feedback loop. The first asks you to calculate fabric delay while respecting the two independent clocks. The second asks which statements correctly connect shared delivery feedback, path-specific credit, and the newer scheduler.

Choose one answer for the first question and all applicable answers for the second. Submit each question once to continue in normal learner mode. Correct answers are not required, and you can retry after reading the feedback. Review the cited specification pages if a distinction is unclear. Take the time to explain why an acknowledgment's congestion metadata cannot replace the saved path identifier of every acknowledged packet.

slides.title: Course complete
slides.transcript:
You have completed module three, Congestion Control and Multipathing, and the full Falcon Transport course. Across the three modules, you traced transactions, explained recovery evidence, and connected congestion measurements to path decisions. You can now follow a measurement through the Rate Update Engine, distinguish fabric and receiver controls, and reason about path selection and protective route changes.

Use the Falcon specification for exact requirements and the related networking courses for broader context. Their mechanisms remain specific to their own transports. Thank you for working through the examples. In your next protocol discussion, trace one packet's measurement, delivery state, and path credit separately before drawing a conclusion about the connection.

lms_catalog.short_description: Trace Falcon transactions, loss recovery, congestion control and multipathing with worked packet flows from v1.2.0.
lms_catalog.overview: Build a transport-level model of Falcon from specification v1.2.0. Follow worked push and pull exchanges, interpret delivery feedback and loss recovery, and connect delay measurements to congestion control and multipathing. Nine animated packet flows and six page-cited knowledge-check questions develop the distinctions between transaction completion, packet acknowledgement and path credit. Examine v1.2 changes and backward compatibility, with references to related OCP Academy networking courses and Summit recordings. Upper-layer protocol mappings and implementation details remain outside scope.
